questions.question: A patient has painful focal cervical dystonia interfering with work. Which treatment is generally preferred for targeted symptomatic control?
options: Botulinum neurotoxin injection into appropriately selected overactive muscles
Chronic high-dose trihexyphenidyl as the default before local treatment
Levodopa as uniformly effective for all adult cervical dystonia
Immediate GPi DBS before an adequate focal treatment trial
questions.explanation:
Botulinum Toxin for Cervical Dystonia

Correct answer: Botulinum neurotoxin injection into appropriately selected overactive muscles

Targeted Neuromuscular Treatment

**Botulinum neurotoxin** reduces acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction and is a standard treatment for focal cervical dystonia. Type A toxins act on SNAP-25; type B acts on synaptobrevin/VAMP.

Select muscles according to the actual dystonic pattern, not simply the direction the head appears to face. EMG or ultrasound guidance can help in appropriate cases.

Dose and distribution are individualized by muscle, severity, prior response and formulation. Units from different toxin products are not directly interchangeable.

Adverse Effects and Follow-up

**Dysphagia and neck weakness** are important local adverse effects, particularly with certain muscle patterns and injection distributions. Counsel about rare distant toxin effects and evaluate breathing or swallowing difficulty promptly.

Benefits are temporary; follow-up and reinjection timing depend on clinical response and product guidance, often around twelve-week intervals rather than a universal identical schedule.

If response is poor, reassess diagnosis, muscle selection, dose, contracture and technique before assuming antibody-mediated resistance. Rehabilitation and pain management complement the injection strategy.

Chronic high-dose trihexyphenidyl as the default before local treatment: Anticholinergics can help selected dystonia, especially some younger generalized cases, but systemic cognitive and autonomic effects often limit them relative to focal injection treatment.

Levodopa as uniformly effective for all adult cervical dystonia: A levodopa trial is important in suspected dopa-responsive presentations, but most isolated adult cervical dystonia does not show that characteristic dramatic sustained response.

Immediate GPi DBS before an adequate focal treatment trial: GPi DBS can help severe medically refractory dystonia, but is generally considered after appropriate less invasive treatment, including optimized focal injections where indicated.

AAN botulinum neurotoxin guideline update, 2016 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4862245/

questions.question: Hours after haloperidol, a young adult develops painful torticollis and sustained upward eye deviation while remaining conscious. There is no generalized clonus or hyperthermia. Which acute treatment is appropriate?
options: Additional haloperidol to suppress the eye and neck movements
Propranolol as the preferred immediate reversal treatment
Parenteral benztropine or diphenhydramine, with airway assessment and withdrawal of the provoking drug
VMAT2 inhibition as the immediate emergency treatment
questions.explanation:
Acute Dopamine-Blocker-Induced Dystonia

Correct answer: Parenteral benztropine or diphenhydramine, with airway assessment and withdrawal of the provoking drug

Acute Extrapyramidal Reaction

**Acute dystonia** can occur soon after a dopamine blocker, especially in younger patients. Oculogyric crisis, jaw/tongue spasm and torticollis are characteristic presentations.

Assess the airway because laryngeal involvement can be life threatening. Preserve a broad differential if consciousness, systemic features or the movement pattern is atypical.

Review antipsychotics and antiemetics such as metoclopramide. Stop or replace the provoking agent with appropriate clinical coordination.

Reversal and Recurrence Prevention

**Adult rescue options include ==benztropine 1–2 mg IM/IV== or ==diphenhydramine 25–50 mg IM/IV==**, according to availability and local protocol. Improvement is usually rapid, especially intravenously.

A short oral anticholinergic/antihistaminic continuation is often needed because the provoking drug can outlast the rescue dose. Reassess promptly if response is incomplete or symptoms recur.

Benzodiazepines may be adjunctive in selected persistent cases. Distinguish this acute reaction from akathisia, tardive syndromes, seizure, tetany and neuroleptic malignant syndrome, because their treatment priorities differ.

Additional haloperidol to suppress the eye and neck movements: Further dopamine blockade can intensify acute dystonia; the temporal relationship and preserved awareness favor a medication reaction requiring reversal.

Propranolol as the preferred immediate reversal treatment: Propranolol is used in selected akathisia or tremor contexts, but does not rapidly reverse the cholinergic–dopaminergic imbalance of an acute dystonic reaction.

VMAT2 inhibition as the immediate emergency treatment: VMAT2 inhibitors can treat tardive dyskinesia or Huntington chorea, but are not the rapid first-line rescue for an acute dystonic reaction.

Indian clinical practice guidance for psychotropic medication emergencies, 2022 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9122152/

questions.question: A girl develops foot inversion and gait difficulty that worsen through the day and improve after sleep. Cognition and sensory examination are preserved. Which therapeutic diagnostic step is most appropriate?
options: Start a VMAT2 inhibitor to deplete dopamine
Treat only with botulinum toxin without evaluating a dopamine-synthesis disorder
A supervised low-dose levodopa/decarboxylase-inhibitor trial
Proceed directly to GPi DBS without a medication trial
questions.explanation:
Dopa-Responsive Dystonia

Correct answer: A supervised low-dose levodopa/decarboxylase-inhibitor trial

Dopamine-Synthesis Defect

**GCH1-deficient dopa-responsive dystonia** commonly causes childhood lower-limb dystonia, diurnal fluctuation and a marked sustained levodopa response. GCH1 encodes GTP cyclohydrolase 1, important for tetrahydrobiopterin synthesis.

The common form is autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance. Other dopamine-synthesis disorders can produce related or more complex phenotypes, so treatment response alone does not identify the gene.

The presentation may be mistaken for cerebral palsy or a spastic gait disorder. Absence of a family history does not exclude it.

Trial and Long-Term Care

**Start levodopa cautiously with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor.** GeneReviews gives an example initiation of ==25–50 mg levodopa one to three times daily== in children aged six years or older, with slow adjustment.

Many classic GCH1 cases achieve a complete or near-complete sustained response at relatively low doses. Transient initial dyskinesia can occur, while typical PD-like long-term fluctuations are uncommon in the classic phenotype.

Arrange appropriate genetic evaluation and counselling. A negative or incomplete initial trial requires review of dose, duration, adherence and alternative diagnoses rather than an automatic conclusion from a single dose.

Start a VMAT2 inhibitor to deplete dopamine: VMAT2 inhibition can help chorea or tardive dyskinesia, but dopamine depletion is not the appropriate mechanistic approach to suspected dopamine-synthesis deficiency.

Treat only with botulinum toxin without evaluating a dopamine-synthesis disorder: Focal injection may reduce a particular posture, but the childhood onset and diurnal pattern warrant a potentially transformative levodopa trial before limiting treatment to local symptoms.

Proceed directly to GPi DBS without a medication trial: DBS may help refractory dystonia, but suspected dopa-responsive disease should first receive a levodopa trial because a low-dose medical response can be dramatic.

questions.question: An asymptomatic adult receives a confirmed HTT result of 38 CAG repeats during a formal predictive-testing programme. Which counselling interpretation is most appropriate?
options: A normal-range allele without a Huntington-related reproductive implication
An intermediate allele with transmission instability but not the conventional disease-associated range
A full-penetrance allele with the same interpretation as a 45-repeat result
This is a reduced-penetrance disease-associated allele; clinical disease is possible but not inevitable
questions.explanation:
Huntington Repeat Ranges

Correct answer: This is a reduced-penetrance disease-associated allele; clinical disease is possible but not inevitable

Conventional Laboratory Categories

**HTT CAG expansion** causes autosomal dominant Huntington disease. Conventional ranges are normal at 26 or fewer, intermediate at ==27–35==, reduced penetrance at ==36–39== and full penetrance at 40 or more repeats.

These categories do not replace assay interpretation. Repeat interruptions and technical methods can affect an estimate near a boundary, so discordant clinical and laboratory findings warrant expert review.

Repeat instability and anticipation are particularly associated with paternal transmission; larger expansions can be associated with juvenile presentations.

Predictive Testing and Family Care

**A result is not merely a laboratory fact.** Pre- and post-test genetic counselling, informed consent, psychological support and discussion of reproductive options are essential.

A heterozygous carrier has a 50% chance of transmitting the allele at each conception, while the transmitted repeat length and penetrance may vary.

Clinical evaluation addresses cognition, behavior, mood, motor function and family support. Do not use a CAG count to make an unsupported exact prediction of employment capacity, lifespan or age of onset.

CAG repeats | Conventional interpretation

≤26 | Normal

27–35 | Intermediate; possible transmission instability

36–39 | Reduced penetrance

≥40 | Full-penetrance disease-associated range within a usual lifespan

An intermediate allele with transmission instability but not the conventional disease-associated range: Intermediate alleles conventionally contain 27–35 repeats; 38 is within the reduced-penetrance disease-associated range and requires different counselling.

A full-penetrance allele with the same interpretation as a 45-repeat result: Forty or more repeats is the conventional full-penetrance range. A 38-repeat result cannot be assigned the same penetrance expectation.

questions.question: A patient with Huntington disease has distressing chorea, active psychosis and inadequately treated major depression. Which strategy is most appropriate?
options: Use an anticholinergic as the preferred treatment for both psychosis and chorea
Start tetrabenazine without first addressing the depression
Treat chorea with levodopa as the routine first choice in this hyperkinetic presentation
Address psychiatric illness urgently and consider a suitable antipsychotic that may also reduce chorea
questions.explanation:
Huntington Chorea with Psychiatric Comorbidity

Correct answer: Address psychiatric illness urgently and consider a suitable antipsychotic that may also reduce chorea

Choose Treatment Around the Whole Syndrome

**Chorea treatment is indicated when movement impairs function, safety or comfort**, not simply because it is visible. Assess mood, suicidality, psychosis, swallowing and falls before choosing a dopamine-reducing agent.

A suitable second-generation antipsychotic may address psychosis and reduce chorea. Sedation, metabolic effects, QT risk and drug-induced parkinsonism require monitoring.

Active depression and suicide risk need direct treatment and support; medication choice should not focus on the motor examination while ignoring psychiatric danger.

VMAT2 Inhibitors

**Tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine and valbenazine** reduce vesicular monoamine storage and have chorea indications in relevant jurisdictions. Their doses, interactions and warnings differ.

Tetrabenazine commonly starts at ==12.5 mg daily== with gradual titration; CYP2D6 testing is required before exceeding ==50 mg/day== under the cited label. Depression/suicidality, sedation, akathisia and parkinsonism are important risks.

Valbenazine also has a Huntington-related depression/suicidality boxed warning. Symptomatic improvement does not establish disease modification; rehabilitation, nutrition, speech/swallowing care and family support remain necessary.

Use an anticholinergic as the preferred treatment for both psychosis and chorea: Anticholinergics do not treat psychosis and can worsen cognition; their selected dystonia/tremor uses do not make them appropriate for this combination.

Start tetrabenazine without first addressing the depression: Tetrabenazine is useful for chorea in appropriate patients but is contraindicated with active suicidality or untreated/inadequately treated depression under its US label.

Treat chorea with levodopa as the routine first choice in this hyperkinetic presentation: Levodopa may have a role in selected rigid juvenile phenotypes but is not the usual treatment for prominent adult chorea and may worsen hyperkinetic or psychotic symptoms.

questions.question: After years of dopamine-blocking antipsychotic treatment, a patient develops persistent oro-bucco-lingual stereotypies and choreiform limb movements. Which targeted drug class has an established role for troublesome tardive dyskinesia?
options: VMAT2 inhibitors such as valbenazine or deutetrabenazine
Anticholinergics as routine treatment for the oro-lingual dyskinesia
Higher-dose dopamine blockade solely to mask the movements long term
Levodopa as the standard treatment for antipsychotic-related stereotypies
questions.explanation:
Tardive Dyskinesia

Correct answer: VMAT2 inhibitors such as valbenazine or deutetrabenazine

A Delayed Drug-Associated Syndrome

**Tardive dyskinesia** follows exposure to dopamine-receptor-blocking drugs and may persist after withdrawal. Orofacial stereotypies, chorea and other movement phenotypes can occur.

Differentiate acute dystonia, akathisia, drug-induced parkinsonism, edentulous movements and other causes. A structured scale such as AIMS helps document distribution and change but does not alone establish etiology.

Review whether the provoking drug is still needed and whether a lower-risk alternative is feasible, while avoiding destabilization of the psychiatric illness.

Targeted Therapy

**Valbenazine and deutetrabenazine** have randomized evidence and relevant regulatory approvals for TD. Use product-specific titration and review CYP interactions, QT risk, sedation and parkinsonism.

Valbenazine for TD commonly starts at ==40 mg once daily== and may increase after one week, with 60 or 80 mg options according to response, tolerability and labeling. Interaction or organ-function restrictions can require lower dosing.

Treatment can improve movement severity but does not guarantee permanent reversal. Coordinate neurological and psychiatric follow-up and assess speech, chewing, swallowing and social function, not only the numerical movement score.

Anticholinergics as routine treatment for the oro-lingual dyskinesia: Anticholinergics can reverse acute dystonia or help selected drug-induced parkinsonism, but may worsen classical tardive dyskinesia and are not its routine targeted therapy.

Higher-dose dopamine blockade solely to mask the movements long term: Increasing blockade may transiently mask dyskinesia but adds exposure and adverse effects; it is not a preferred disease-management strategy for persistent troublesome TD.

Levodopa as the standard treatment for antipsychotic-related stereotypies: Levodopa is used for selected hypodopaminergic motor syndromes and is not a standard treatment for the described tardive hyperkinetic syndrome.

questions.question: A 22-year-old has dysarthria, dystonia and an irregular proximal action tremor. Liver enzymes are mildly abnormal. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
options: Liver ultrasound and routine liver enzymes as the principal exclusion tests
Serum ceruloplasmin and total copper alone, followed by a decision without further testing
Brain MRI and a levodopa-response trial as the principal confirmation tests
Slit-lamp examination, ceruloplasmin, basal 24-hour urinary copper and integrated clinical/genetic assessment
questions.explanation:
Neurological Wilson Disease: Composite Diagnosis

Correct answer: Slit-lamp examination, ceruloplasmin, basal 24-hour urinary copper and integrated clinical/genetic assessment

Recognizing a Treatable Cause

**Wilson disease is an ATP7B-related recessive disorder of copper handling.** Young-onset mixed movement disorder, dysarthria, psychiatric change or unexplained liver disease should prompt evaluation.

Kayser–Fleischer rings are common in neurological presentations but not universal. Slit-lamp assessment is more appropriate than relying on an unaided bedside inspection.

Brain MRI can show basal-ganglia and brainstem abnormalities, but neither a normal scan nor absence of a famous imaging sign excludes the disease.

Copper Tests and Confirmation

**Ceruloplasmin is often low**, with values below about ==14 mg/dL== particularly suggestive, but sensitivity and specificity are imperfect. Low values occur in other conditions.

Basal 24-hour urinary copper is commonly above ==100 µg/day== in symptomatic disease. Lower values do not categorically exclude early disease, while other liver disorders can also increase excretion.

Integrate ophthalmic, neurological, hepatic, biochemical and ATP7B findings, often using a Leipzig-based framework. Liver copper quantification or newer exchangeable-copper tests may help selected unresolved cases according to availability and specialist expertise.

Liver ultrasound and routine liver enzymes as the principal exclusion tests: These assess hepatic structure and injury but may be nonspecific or relatively mild in neurological Wilson disease; they cannot replace specific copper and ophthalmic studies.

Serum ceruloplasmin and total copper alone, followed by a decision without further testing: These are useful components, but neither normal ceruloplasmin nor low total copper independently rules disease out or in; the young neurological phenotype warrants a composite assessment.

Brain MRI and a levodopa-response trial as the principal confirmation tests: MRI can support the differential and a levodopa trial may help selected symptoms, but neither confirms ATP7B-related copper disease or replaces copper and ophthalmic evaluation.

questions.question: A patient with neurological Wilson disease is starting chelation. Which treatment principle is most appropriate?
options: Use a specialist-guided start-low, go-slow regimen and monitor neurological status and copper balance
Begin full-dose penicillamine immediately rather than gradual introduction
Choose zinc monotherapy without first assessing the severity of hepatic involvement
Switch to dietary copper restriction alone once the first clinical improvement occurs
questions.explanation:
Treating Neurological Wilson Disease

Correct answer: Use a specialist-guided start-low, go-slow regimen and monitor neurological status and copper balance

Copper Removal and Absorption Reduction

**Penicillamine and trientine are copper chelators**, while zinc induces intestinal metallothionein and reduces copper absorption. Selection depends on neurological and hepatic severity, prior response and tolerability.

EASL-ERN 2025 recommends either zinc or a chelator for a neurological presentation, with start-low, go-slow chelator initiation. Significant liver involvement favors chelation rather than assuming zinc is sufficient.

Adult penicillamine often reaches ==750–1500 mg/day== in divided doses; gradual initiation is important in neurological disease. Trientine doses depend on the salt/formulation and should not be exchanged milligram for milligram.

Monitoring and Safety

**Neurological deterioration, undertreatment and copper deficiency** must all be considered during follow-up. Use clinical examination, liver tests, blood counts, urinalysis and properly interpreted copper studies.

Penicillamine can cause rash, cytopenias, proteinuria and autoimmune toxicity; pyridoxine supplementation is commonly provided. Zinc is often prescribed as ==50 mg elemental zinc three times daily== in adults, separated from meals and interacting agents as instructed.

Urinary copper targets differ between initial chelation, maintenance and zinc treatment. Do not apply one universal threshold or interpret copper excretion without knowing the drug, adherence and sampling conditions.

Begin full-dose penicillamine immediately rather than gradual introduction: Penicillamine is a valid chelator, but rapid introduction can increase concern about paradoxical neurological worsening; neurological disease supports cautious escalation and close follow-up.

Choose zinc monotherapy without first assessing the severity of hepatic involvement: Zinc can be appropriate in selected neurological or maintenance settings, but significant liver disease favors chelation; the hepatic assessment is necessary before choosing it.

Switch to dietary copper restriction alone once the first clinical improvement occurs: Dietary measures can complement therapy but do not provide adequate ongoing copper control in established Wilson disease; improvement is not a reason to stop effective anti-copper treatment.

questions.question: A 15-year-old has had several motor tics and a vocal tic intermittently for eighteen months, beginning at age twelve. The motor and vocal tics were not always simultaneous. Drugs and other causes are excluded. Which diagnosis fits best?
options: Provisional tic disorder because tics wax and wane
Persistent motor tic disorder because motor and vocal tics were not simultaneous
Tourette syndrome
Persistent vocal tic disorder despite multiple established motor tics
questions.explanation:
Tourette Syndrome Diagnostic Requirements

Correct answer: Tourette syndrome

Motor, Vocal and Time Criteria

**Tourette syndrome** requires multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic at some point in the illness, not necessarily at the same time, with persistence for more than a year since first tic onset and onset before age eighteen.

Symptoms must not be attributable to a substance or another medical disorder. The pattern commonly waxes and wanes, and temporary improvement does not restart the diagnostic clock.

Coprolalia is not required and occurs in only a minority. Common vocal tics include throat clearing, sniffing and simple sounds.

Clinical Assessment

**Premonitory urges and temporary suppressibility** are common but may be difficult for younger children to describe. Distinguish tics from stereotypies, chorea, dystonia, seizures and functional tic-like behaviors.

Assess impairment and comorbid ADHD, OCD, anxiety and mood symptoms. Comorbidity can cause more disability than the tics themselves.

Treatment is selected according to functional burden rather than the diagnostic label alone. Education and watchful waiting can be appropriate when impairment is minimal, while behavioral or pharmacological treatment is available for troublesome symptoms.

Provisional tic disorder because tics wax and wane: Waxing and waning is common; provisional disorder applies to a shorter duration, not to every fluctuating course lasting more than a year.

Persistent motor tic disorder because motor and vocal tics were not simultaneous: Tourette criteria do not require simultaneity. Persistent motor-only disorder applies when the required vocal component has not occurred.

Persistent vocal tic disorder despite multiple established motor tics: A vocal-only persistent disorder does not capture a history meeting both the multiple-motor and vocal components of Tourette syndrome.

questions.question: A teenager with Tourette syndrome has bothersome tics, wants active treatment and can participate in behavioral sessions. There is no urgent injury risk. Which initial option should be offered when available?
options: Use a VMAT2 inhibitor as a universally established first-line tic therapy
Start haloperidol automatically before discussing behavioral treatment
Comprehensive behavioral intervention for tics
Treat only the visible tics and avoid evaluating ADHD or OCD
questions.explanation:
Choosing Treatment for Troublesome Tics

Correct answer: Comprehensive behavioral intervention for tics

Behavioral Intervention

**CBIT combines habit-reversal elements, awareness training, competing responses and modification of tic-provoking situations.** AAN guidance supports offering it as an initial option relative to medication when appropriate and available.

It is not an instruction simply to suppress symptoms through willpower. Explain the structured skills-based approach and adapt it to age, motivation and access.

Education and school/work accommodations can reduce stigma and environmental burden alongside active treatment.

Medication by Comorbidity and Severity

**Clonidine or guanfacine** can help selected patients, particularly when ADHD coexists. Monitor sedation, BP and HR; taper rather than stopping an alpha-2 agonist abruptly.

Aripiprazole or other appropriate antipsychotics may be used when benefits justify risks. Monitor weight/metabolic effects, akathisia, other drug-induced movements and relevant cardiac risks.

Assess symptom-related disability periodically because tics often change with age and context. The goal is improved function and well-being rather than a promise of complete permanent tic elimination.

Use a VMAT2 inhibitor as a universally established first-line tic therapy: VMAT2 drugs have established roles in TD and Huntington chorea, but should not be assumed to have equivalent evidence or a universal first-line indication for Tourette tics.

Start haloperidol automatically before discussing behavioral treatment: Antipsychotics can reduce severe tics, but their movement, metabolic and other adverse effects make automatic first-line use inappropriate when an evidence-based behavioral option is feasible.

Treat only the visible tics and avoid evaluating ADHD or OCD: Comorbid ADHD and OCD commonly drive impairment and affect treatment choice; ignoring them can leave the major disability untreated.

questions.question: A patient has brief stimulus-sensitive distal jerks. EEG–EMG back-averaging shows a contralateral cortical potential preceding the hand-muscle burst by about 20 ms. Which interpretation is best?
options: The finding supports a cortical generator for the myoclonus
It proves a purely spinal generator
It establishes a functional cause from the short latency alone
It identifies one specific degenerative etiology regardless of the history
questions.explanation:
Electrophysiological Evidence of Cortical Myoclonus

Correct answer: The finding supports a cortical generator for the myoclonus

Generator Localization

**Jerk-locked EEG–EMG back-averaging** can reveal a small cortical transient that is difficult to see in the raw EEG. A hand-muscle latency compatible with corticospinal conduction supports cortical myoclonus.

Brief EMG bursts, stimulus sensitivity and giant somatosensory evoked potentials can provide additional support. Giant potentials alone are not disease-specific and should be integrated with the other findings.

Negative myoclonus is a brief interruption of muscle activity rather than a positive contraction; the physiology and causes require appropriate classification.

Cause-Directed Treatment

**Review drugs, renal/hepatic dysfunction, glucose/electrolytes, hypoxic injury and epileptic or degenerative disease.** Treat a reversible cause before merely suppressing the movement.

Levetiracetam, valproate or clonazepam can help selected cortical myoclonus. For example, levetiracetam may start at ==250–500 mg twice daily== with renal adjustment and titration; monitor mood and sedation.

Valproate requires reproductive and liver-safety assessment, and clonazepam can cause sedation and falls. A drug useful for cortical myoclonus may not help a spinal or subcortical generator, making physiological localization clinically useful.

It proves a purely spinal generator: Spinal myoclonus has different recruitment and physiology; a correctly localized time-locked cortical potential preceding the distal burst supports cortical involvement.

It establishes a functional cause from the short latency alone: A short corticospinal-compatible latency does not establish a functional cause; functional jerks require their own positive clinical and physiological assessment.

It identifies one specific degenerative etiology regardless of the history: Cortical myoclonus is a physiological classification shared by several metabolic, epileptic, posthypoxic, toxic and degenerative disorders; etiology needs further evaluation.

questions.question: A patient has right-sided finger–nose dysmetria, intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia without weakness or proprioceptive loss. Which localization best fits?
options: A purely bilateral vestibular deficit without limb involvement
Left cerebellar hemisphere as the obligatory site because all motor pathways cross once
Right dorsal columns as the primary explanation despite preserved proprioception
Right cerebellar hemisphere or its functional connections
questions.explanation:
Cerebellar Limb and Gait Localization

Correct answer: Right cerebellar hemisphere or its functional connections

Ipsilateral Limb Incoordination

**Cerebellar hemisphere dysfunction** commonly produces ipsilateral limb dysmetria, decomposition, intention tremor and impaired rapid alternating movement.

Vermian or midline dysfunction more prominently affects truncal control and gait. Ocular findings such as gaze-evoked nystagmus and saccadic dysmetria can support cerebellar-system involvement.

Weakness, sensory loss, pain and apraxia can impair coordination tests, so establish that the abnormality reflects incoordination rather than inability to execute the movement.

Localization Does Not Establish Etiology

**The time course directs the next investigation.** Sudden onset raises vascular or toxic concerns; subacute disease suggests immune, infectious, neoplastic or nutritional causes; chronic progression raises degenerative and inherited possibilities.

MRI evaluates cerebellar, brainstem and connected pathways, while targeted laboratory and genetic studies depend on the phenotype. A normal early scan does not exclude every physiological or metabolic cause.

The localization remains useful for urgent decision-making, but should not lead to an automatic hereditary diagnosis or delay acute stroke evaluation when symptoms began abruptly.

A purely bilateral vestibular deficit without limb involvement: Vestibular loss commonly impairs gaze stability and gait but does not by itself explain unilateral limb dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia.

Left cerebellar hemisphere as the obligatory site because all motor pathways cross once: Cerebellar limb signs are usually ipsilateral because of the relevant circuit anatomy; a simple single-crossing rule is inappropriate.

Right dorsal columns as the primary explanation despite preserved proprioception: Sensory ataxia from dorsal-column disease typically includes impaired position sense and greater reliance on vision, which are absent in this focal cerebellar pattern.

questions.question: A patient becomes markedly unsteady in darkness, has absent vibration and position sense in the feet and reduced sensory nerve action potentials. Limb coordination improves with visual guidance. Which mechanism best explains the dominant ataxia?
options: Pure corticospinal tract degeneration
Pure cerebellar hemispheric degeneration without sensory involvement
Isolated bilateral vestibular failure
Loss of proprioceptive afferent input
questions.explanation:
Sensory Versus Vestibular Ataxia

Correct answer: Loss of proprioceptive afferent input

Dependence on Vision

**Sensory ataxia** results from impaired proprioceptive input through peripheral sensory neurons, large fibers or central pathways. Visual guidance partly compensates, so balance worsens when the eyes close.

A positive Romberg sign is not specific for one disease and can also occur with vestibular impairment. Interpret it with sensory testing and ocular/vestibular examination.

Reduced sensory potentials support peripheral sensory involvement; preserved potentials with impaired position sense can suggest a more central pathway lesion, depending on the complete study.

Combined Balance-System Disease

**Bilateral vestibulopathy** produces oscillopsia during head movement and impaired vestibulo-ocular reflexes. Cerebellar disease causes additional ocular and limb signs.

RFC1-related disease can combine all three balance-system impairments, so do not force every patient into one isolated category.

Evaluate treatable causes including nutritional deficiency, toxic exposure, immune sensory neuronopathy and structural cord disease. Rehabilitation should account for sensory substitution, lighting and fall prevention.

Dominant mechanism | Discriminating clues

Cerebellar | Dysmetria, dysarthria, cerebellar ocular signs

Sensory | Position/vibration loss; visual compensation

Bilateral vestibular | Oscillopsia; abnormal head-impulse/VOR testing

Combined | Features from more than one system; consider CANVAS/RFC1

Pure corticospinal tract degeneration: Corticospinal dysfunction causes weakness and upper motor neuron signs; it does not by itself account for this visual compensation and sensory-afferent deficit.

Pure cerebellar hemispheric degeneration without sensory involvement: Cerebellar ataxia can persist despite visual guidance and does not explain the documented proprioceptive and sensory nerve abnormalities.

Isolated bilateral vestibular failure: Bilateral vestibular loss can worsen balance in darkness, but usually produces impaired vestibulo-ocular responses and oscillopsia rather than loss of joint-position sense with abnormal sensory potentials.

questions.question: A hypertensive adult develops sudden vertigo, severe gait/truncal ataxia and dysarthria. An initial noncontrast CT shows no hemorrhage. Which next approach is most appropriate?
options: Treat only with vestibular suppressants and wait several days for improvement
Discharge with a diagnosis of vestibular neuritis because CT is normal
Order an outpatient hereditary ataxia panel before further acute imaging
Continue urgent posterior-circulation stroke evaluation with appropriate vascular and posterior-fossa imaging
questions.explanation:
Acute Cerebellar Ataxia Requires Urgent Assessment

Correct answer: Continue urgent posterior-circulation stroke evaluation with appropriate vascular and posterior-fossa imaging

Posterior Circulation Warning Pattern

**Sudden severe ataxia with dysarthria** warrants urgent stroke assessment. CT is useful for hemorrhage but is relatively insensitive for early posterior-fossa ischemia.

Use vascular imaging and MRI with diffusion sequences according to the acute pathway and clinical circumstances. Even early diffusion MRI can occasionally be falsely negative in posterior-circulation disease.

Do not delay eligible acute treatment solely to obtain a preferred image. Bedside vestibular algorithms require the correct clinical syndrome and trained examination; they are not a universal substitute for stroke assessment.

Deterioration from Cerebellar Infarction

**Swelling can cause brainstem compression and obstructive hydrocephalus.** New reduced consciousness or worsening cranial-nerve/brainstem findings require urgent repeat assessment and neurosurgical input.

CSF diversion may be needed for obstructive hydrocephalus. Neurological deterioration from swelling or persistent compression can require decompressive suboccipital surgery under current AHA/ASA guidance.

Serial examination, airway protection and appropriate monitored care are essential. An initially small clinical deficit does not guarantee a benign posterior-fossa course.

Treat only with vestibular suppressants and wait several days for improvement: Symptom relief does not exclude stroke. Waiting can miss reperfusion opportunities and evolving posterior-fossa swelling or hydrocephalus.

Discharge with a diagnosis of vestibular neuritis because CT is normal: A normal early CT does not reliably exclude posterior-fossa ischemia, and dysarthria with severe truncal/gait ataxia is concerning for a central process.

Order an outpatient hereditary ataxia panel before further acute imaging: Inherited disease usually has a different tempo; genetic testing does not replace time-critical evaluation of abrupt focal neurological dysfunction.

questions.explanation:
Friedreich Ataxia: Multisystem Recognition

Correct answer: Friedreich ataxia

Frataxin Deficiency

**Friedreich ataxia** is usually caused by biallelic intronic GAA expansions in FXN, reducing frataxin and impairing mitochondrial iron–sulfur biology. Less common alleles include sequence variants or deletions.

The classic phenotype combines cerebellar/sensory ataxia, areflexia and pyramidal signs. Retained reflexes and late-onset forms exist, so absence of a single classic sign does not exclude FRDA.

SCA6

questions.explanation:
A Discriminating Clue in Dominant SCA

Correct answer: SCA2

Phenotype-Guided Genetic Testing

**SCA2 is an ATXN2 CAG-repeat disorder** with autosomal dominant inheritance. Slow saccades, ataxia, dysarthria and neuropathy are useful clinical clues.

Phenotypic overlap is substantial, and some SCA2 cases present with levodopa-responsive parkinsonism. A bedside clue guides testing rather than proving the subtype.

Anticipation can occur in repeat disorders, but family-specific counselling depends on the gene and repeat behavior.

Common Comparisons

**SCA1** often has prominent pyramidal/bulbar involvement; **SCA3** can have mixed pyramidal, extrapyramidal and peripheral features; **SCA6** is often relatively pure cerebellar disease; **SCA7** adds retinal degeneration.

Choose a validated repeat-expansion strategy rather than assuming all common SCAs are excluded by a sequence-only panel. Review exactly which loci and repeat structures the laboratory assesses.

Assess swallowing, mobility, neuropathy, vision and family support according to the phenotype. Subtype identification informs prognosis and family counselling even when treatment remains mainly symptomatic.

Subtype | Gene | Useful clue

SCA1 | ATXN1 | Pyramidal/bulbar signs

SCA2 | ATXN2 | Marked slow saccades; neuropathy

SCA3 | ATXN3 | Mixed pyramidal/extrapyramidal/peripheral findings

SCA6 | CACNA1A | Relatively pure cerebellar phenotype

SCA7 | ATXN7 | Retinal degeneration/visual loss

SCA6: SCA6 commonly produces a relatively pure cerebellar syndrome with nystagmus; marked slow saccades and neuropathy more strongly suggest SCA2, though overlap exists.

SCA7: SCA7 is especially associated with retinal degeneration and visual loss; slow saccades can occur but are less discriminating than the characteristic retinal phenotype.

SCA3: SCA3 can combine ataxia, pyramidal/extrapyramidal signs and neuropathy, but exceptionally slow saccades are a particularly useful SCA2 clue; genetic testing is still necessary.

questions.question: A 69-year-old man has intention tremor, gait ataxia and neuropathy. MRI shows middle cerebellar peduncle white-matter abnormalities. His daughter has premature ovarian insufficiency. Which test is most relevant?
options: FMR1 CGG-repeat analysis for a premutation
HTT CAG-repeat testing as the leading explanation of this phenotype
FXN expansion analysis as the only appropriate late-onset test
A conventional karyotype alone to detect the relevant repeat size
questions.explanation:
Fragile X-Associated Tremor/Ataxia Syndrome

Correct answer: FMR1 CGG-repeat analysis for a premutation

Premutation-Associated Disease

**FXTAS** most often affects older FMR1 premutation carriers, particularly men, with action/intention tremor, gait ataxia and variable neuropathy, parkinsonism or cognitive/autonomic features.

The premutation range is approximately ==55–200 CGG repeats==. This differs from the usually methylated full mutation associated with fragile X syndrome.

Middle cerebellar peduncle signal change is a useful imaging clue but is not uniquely diagnostic and is less consistently present in affected women.

Family Implications

**FMR1 premutations also confer risk of fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency** in women. A pedigree may therefore link late-life ataxia with reproductive or neurodevelopmental findings in relatives.

Premutation carriers do not all develop FXTAS; penetrance varies with age, sex and repeat-related factors. Genetic counselling should address transmission patterns and the possibility of expansion through maternal transmission.

Care is mainly supportive and symptom directed, including mobility, cognition, neuropathy and autonomic assessment. Do not equate a carrier result with a guaranteed neurological prognosis.

HTT CAG-repeat testing as the leading explanation of this phenotype: HTT testing is relevant to Huntington phenotypes with chorea and cognitive/behavioral change; the tremor–ataxia plus ovarian family history points toward an FMR1 premutation.

FXN expansion analysis as the only appropriate late-onset test: FRDA can occasionally be late onset, but this specific family and middle-peduncle pattern favors FXTAS; testing should follow the complete phenotype.

A conventional karyotype alone to detect the relevant repeat size: A karyotype does not provide the molecular repeat sizing and methylation-related information used to classify FMR1 alleles.

questions.question: A 62-year-old has slowly progressive ataxia, a sensory neuronopathy, bilateral vestibular hypofunction and a chronic unexplained cough predating imbalance. A sequence-only exome was negative. Which next test is most appropriate?
options: Targeted testing for biallelic pathogenic RFC1 repeat expansions
FMR1 CGG-repeat analysis
FGF14 GAA-repeat analysis
FXN GAA-repeat analysis
questions.explanation:
RFC1-Related CANVAS

Correct answer: Targeted testing for biallelic pathogenic RFC1 repeat expansions

Three Balance Systems

**CANVAS** combines cerebellar ataxia, sensory neuropathy/neuronopathy and bilateral vestibular areflexia. RFC1-related disease can also involve only part of this spectrum.

Chronic cough can precede neurological symptoms by years. Vestibular loss causes oscillopsia and impaired vestibulo-ocular responses; sensory neuronopathy can markedly worsen balance in darkness.

Autonomic symptoms may occur and should not automatically redirect the diagnosis to MSA.

Testing the Molecular Mechanism

**Biallelic intronic RFC1 repeat expansions** are a major cause. The common pathogenic motif is AAGGG, but additional pathogenic repeat configurations exist and test coverage matters.

Conventional sequence-based panels or exomes do not reliably exclude the expansion. Use a validated repeat assay and discuss unresolved cases with the laboratory or a neurogenetics service.

Provide gait and vestibular rehabilitation, sensory-compensation advice, swallowing assessment and cough/autonomic care as needed. A recessive adult-onset disorder can occur without an obvious family history.

FMR1 CGG-repeat analysis: FMR1 testing is relevant for late-onset tremor–ataxia, especially with a fragile-X/ovarian family history, but the sensory-neuronopathy, vestibular and cough combination particularly favors RFC1.

FGF14 GAA-repeat analysis: FGF14 expansions can cause late-onset cerebellar disease, often with episodic exacerbations and downbeat nystagmus; marked sensory neuronopathy and vestibular failure with cough more specifically suggest RFC1.

FXN GAA-repeat analysis: FRDA can be late onset and combines sensory and cerebellar dysfunction, but the full vestibular–cough CANVAS pattern makes targeted RFC1 testing the stronger next choice.

questions.question: A 65-year-old has gradually progressive gait ataxia with episodic worsening after alcohol or exertion and downbeat nystagmus. Common SCA expansion testing and routine exome sequencing are unrevealing. Which recently recognized cause should be specifically assessed?
options: Biallelic RFC1 expansions
GAA-repeat expansion in FGF14, also called SCA27B
An FMR1 premutation
Biallelic FXN expansions
questions.explanation:
FGF14 GAA-Expansion Ataxia

Correct answer: GAA-repeat expansion in FGF14, also called SCA27B

Late-Onset Expansion Disorder

**GAA-FGF14-related ataxia** often causes slowly progressive adult-onset cerebellar gait dysfunction, downbeat nystagmus and episodic exacerbations, sometimes triggered by alcohol or exertion.

It is an autosomal dominant intronic expansion disorder. Expansions above 300 repeats are generally considered fully penetrant; ==250–300 repeats== have reduced penetrance and require careful clinical and family interpretation.

A routine exome or a historical panel that omitted the expansion does not exclude it. Confirm the laboratory’s repeat-detection method and coverage.

Counselling and Symptomatic Care

**Clinical phenotype and segregation matter**, especially in a reduced-penetrance range. Do not treat every borderline expansion as a complete explanation without considering other causes.

Preliminary studies suggest symptomatic benefit from 4-aminopyridine for selected symptoms, including downbeat nystagmus, but this should not be described as proven disease modification or a universal approved indication.

Review seizure history, renal function and formulation-specific safety before considering an aminopyridine. Rehabilitation, fall prevention and trigger counselling remain important while longer-term therapeutic evidence evolves.

Biallelic RFC1 expansions: RFC1 disease is a major late-onset ataxia cause, but prominent sensory neuronopathy, bilateral vestibular impairment and chronic cough would strengthen it; episodic worsening and downbeat nystagmus are useful FGF14 clues.

An FMR1 premutation: FXTAS can cause late-onset tremor and ataxia, particularly in men, with neuropathy and characteristic family/MRI clues; the described episodic cerebellar/ocular phenotype particularly suggests FGF14 expansion disease.

Biallelic FXN expansions: Late-onset FRDA is possible, but a sensory-pyramidal syndrome and relevant systemic manifestations would be more supportive than the predominantly episodic/downbeat pattern here.

questions.question: A young adult has a Friedreich-like ataxia with sensory loss and areflexia, but FXN testing is negative. Which readily actionable investigation should not be omitted?
options: Serum anti-Yo testing as the leading test without a rapid acquired course
FMR1 premutation testing as the most directly actionable first screen
Dopamine-transporter SPECT as the principal biochemical investigation
Vitamin E assessment interpreted with the lipid profile
questions.explanation:
Treatable Causes of Progressive Ataxia

Correct answer: Vitamin E assessment interpreted with the lipid profile

Vitamin E Deficiency as a Mimic

**Ataxia with vitamin E deficiency** can resemble FRDA and may result from malabsorption or TTPA-related disease. Interpret alpha-tocopherol in relation to lipid status rather than an isolated concentration alone.

Timely replacement can stabilize or improve selected manifestations, especially before advanced irreversible injury. Investigate the underlying cause and monitor response and biochemical levels.

The presence of a hereditary phenotype does not exclude a treatable metabolic disorder.

For confirmed AVED, reported adult replacement regimens use ==800–1500 mg/day== of oral vitamin E, adjusted to the preparation and biochemical response under specialist supervision. Do not interchange milligrams and international units without accounting for the formulation.

Broader Reversible-Cause Screen

**B12 and copper deficiency, thyroid disease, alcohol and medications** are important additional causes or contributors. Phenytoin, lithium and sedative toxicity should be considered from the exposure history.

Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy needs prompt parenteral thiamine rather than waiting for a vitamin result. Correct hypoglycemia immediately while arranging thiamine; do not delay lifesaving glucose.

For possible celiac/gluten-related disease, obtain appropriate serology, including total IgA with IgA-based testing, before dietary exclusion when feasible. Immune and nutritional evaluations should be phenotype guided rather than a nonspecific antibody panel replacing clinical reasoning.

Serum anti-Yo testing as the leading test without a rapid acquired course: Anti-Yo evaluation can be relevant to rapidly progressive paraneoplastic cerebellar disease; the stated young FRDA-like phenotype more directly supports a metabolic/nutritional screen.

FMR1 premutation testing as the most directly actionable first screen: FXTAS testing is appropriate in an older tremor–ataxia phenotype or a suggestive family, whereas a young FRDA-like sensory syndrome warrants checking a treatable vitamin E deficiency.

Dopamine-transporter SPECT as the principal biochemical investigation: DAT imaging is useful in selected uncertain parkinsonism/tremor cases, but does not detect a nutritional cause of sensory-pyramidal ataxia.

Guidelines on diagnosis and management of progressive ataxias, 2019 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6381619/

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman develops severe gait and limb ataxia over six weeks. MRI is initially near normal. Anti-Yo/PCA-1 is confirmed with an appropriate assay. Which next priority is most appropriate?
options: Order a hereditary ataxia panel before considering acquired causes
Repeat MRI only after several months before beginning a tumor search
Investigate a compatible underlying malignancy, particularly breast or gynecological cancer, while assessing other causes and treatment
Treat as nonparaneoplastic autoimmune ataxia without malignancy screening
questions.explanation:
Rapidly Progressive Paraneoplastic Cerebellar Syndrome

Correct answer: Investigate a compatible underlying malignancy, particularly breast or gynecological cancer, while assessing other causes and treatment

High-Risk Phenotype and Antibody

**Rapidly progressive cerebellar syndrome** is a high-risk paraneoplastic phenotype in the 2021 criteria. Anti-Yo is strongly associated with breast and gynecological malignancies.

Other associations include DNER/Tr with Hodgkin lymphoma and Hu with small-cell lung cancer, often with additional neurological involvement. These are associations, not a substitute for confirmation.

Verify unexpected results with appropriate methods because commercial panels can produce false positives, particularly when the phenotype is discordant.

Evaluation and Management

**Search for and treat the tumor promptly**, while excluding direct CNS tumor involvement, infection, toxic/metabolic causes and nonparaneoplastic autoimmunity.

For a high-risk phenotype with a high-risk antibody and initially negative cancer screening, the 2021 panel recommends repeat screening ==every four to six months for two years==, individualized to the clinical context.

Immunotherapy may be considered with specialist input, but responses to intracellular-antigen syndromes such as anti-Yo can be limited because neuronal injury may be irreversible. Rehabilitation, swallowing and nutrition care should start alongside the etiologic workup.

Order a hereditary ataxia panel before considering acquired causes: Genetic testing can help unexplained chronic ataxia, but the six-week course and confirmed anti-Yo result prioritize acquired and cancer-associated evaluation.

Repeat MRI only after several months before beginning a tumor search: Follow-up MRI may show evolution, but waiting for atrophy can delay investigation of a high-risk antibody and rapidly progressive phenotype that already justify cancer screening.

Treat as nonparaneoplastic autoimmune ataxia without malignancy screening: Some immune ataxias are nonparaneoplastic, but anti-Yo is a high-risk cancer-associated antibody; immunotherapy should not displace the tumor search.

Updated diagnostic criteria for paraneoplastic neurological syndromes, 2021 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8237398/
